claim: The extinct 'New World stilt-legged' (NWSL) equids are a group of Pleistocene horses endemic to North America.
source: The extinct 'New World stilt-legged', or NWSL, equids constitute a perplexing group of Pleistocene horses endemic to North America.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of NWSL equids.

claim: NWSL equids have slender distal limb bones that resemble those of Asiatic asses, such as the Persian onager.
source: Their slender distal limb bones resemble those of Asiatic asses, such as the Persian onager.
evidence: This morphological observation is stated in the abstract.

claim: Previous palaeogenetic studies have suggested a closer relationship of NWSL equids to caballine horses than to Asiatic asses.
source: Previous palaeogenetic studies, however, have suggested a closer relationship to caballine horses than to Asiatic asses.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior research findings.

claim: Multiple NWSL equid species have been named.
source: Although multiple NWSL equid species have been named, our palaeogenomic and morphometric analyses support the idea that there was only a single species of middle to late Pleistocene NWSL equid
evidence: This is stated as background information in the abstract.

claim: Palaeogenomic and morphometric analyses support the idea that there was only a single species of middle to late Pleistocene NWSL equid.
source: Although multiple NWSL equid species have been named, our palaeogenomic and morphometric analyses support the idea that there was only a single species of middle to late Pleistocene NWSL equid
evidence: This is a primary finding based on the analyses conducted in this study.

claim: NWSL equids fall outside of crown group Equus.
source: and demonstrate that it falls outside of crown group Equus.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the phylogenetic analyses presented in the study.

claim: A new genus, Haringtonhippus, is proposed for the sole species H. francisci.
source: We therefore propose a new genus, Haringtonhippus, for the sole species H. francisci.
evidence: This is a taxonomic conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: The family Equidae has a ~55 million year evolutionary history from dog-sized hyracotheres to present-day Equus.
source: The family that includes modern horses, asses, and zebras, the Equidae, is a classic model of macroevolution. The excellent fossil record of this family clearly documents its ~55 million year evolution from dog-sized hyracotheres through many intermediate forms and extinct offshoots to present-day Equus, which comprises all living equid species (MacFadden, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to MacFadden, 1992.

claim: Many dubious fossil equid taxa have been erected, especially within Pleistocene Equus of North America.
source: The downside of this excellent fossil record is that many dubious fossil equid taxa have been erected, a problem especially acute within Pleistocene Equus of North America (Macdonald et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Macdonald et al., 1992.

claim: Molecular data suggest that most Pleistocene North American equids belonged to, or were closely related to, a single, highly variable stout-legged caballine species that includes the domestic horse, E. caballus.
source: While numerous species are described from the fossil record, molecular data suggest that most belonged to, or were closely related to, a single, highly variable stout-legged caballine species that includes the domestic horse, E. caballus (Weinstock et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Weinstock et al., 2005.

claim: NWSL equids exhibit slender, stilt-like distal limb bones with narrow hooves reminiscent of extant Eurasian hemionines.
source: The enigmatic and extinct 'New World stilt-legged' (NWSL) forms, however, exhibit a perplexing mix of morphological characters, including slender, stilt-like distal limb bones with narrow hooves reminiscent of extant Eurasian hemionines, the Asiatic wild asses (E. hemionus, E. kiang) (Eisenmann, 1992; Eisenmann et al., 2008; Harington and Clulow, 1973; Lundelius and Stevens, 1970; Scott, 2004)
evidence: This morphological description is supported by multiple citations.

claim: NWSL equid dentitions have been interpreted as more consistent with either caballine horses or hemionines.
source: and dentitions that have been interpreted as more consistent with either caballine horses (Lundelius and Stevens, 1970) or hemionines (MacFadden, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to different interpretations in the literature.

claim: NWSL equids have traditionally been considered as allied to hemionines based on their slender distal limb bones.
source: On the basis of their slender distal limb bones, the NWSL equids have traditionally been considered as allied to hemionines (e.g. Eisenmann et al., 2008; Guthrie, 2003; Scott, 2004; Skinner and Hibbard, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Palaeogenetic analyses based on mitochondrial DNA have consistently placed NWSL equids closer to caballine horses.
source: Palaeogenetic analyses based on mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) have, however, consistently placed NWSL equids closer to caballine horses (Barrón-Ortiz et al., 2017; Der Sarkissian et al., 2015; Orlando et al., 2008, 2009; Vilstrup et al., 2013; Weinstock et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous palaeogenetic studies.

claim: The current mtDNA-based phylogenetic model suggests that the stilt-legged morphology arose independently in the New and Old Worlds.
source: The current mtDNA-based phylogenetic model therefore suggests that the stilt-legged morphology arose independently in the New and Old Worlds (Weinstock et al., 2005)
evidence: This is an inference from previous studies, supported by a citation.

claim: The stilt-legged morphology may represent convergent adaptations to arid climates and habitats.
source: and may represent convergent adaptations to arid climates and habitats (Eisenmann, 1985).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by a citation.

claim: Previous phylogenetic models have been based on 15 short control region sequences (<1000 base pairs).
source: However, these models have been based on two questionable sources. The first is based on 15 short control region sequences (<1000 base pairs, bp; Barrón-Ortiz et al., 2017; Weinstock et al., 2005)
evidence: This is a description of previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Short control region sequences can be unreliable for resolving the placement of major equid groups.
source: a data type that can be unreliable for resolving the placement of major equid groups (Der Sarkissian et al., 2015; Orlando et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies discussing methodological limitations.

claim: The earliest recognized NWSL equid fossils date to the late Pliocene/early Pleistocene (~2–3 million years ago) of New Mexico.
source: The earliest recognized NWSL equid fossils date to the late Pliocene/early Pleistocene (~2–3 million years ago, Ma) of New Mexico (Azzaroli and Voorhies, 1993; Eisenmann, 2003; Eisenmann et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to paleontological studies.

claim: Middle and late Pleistocene NWSL equids tended to be smaller in stature than their early Pleistocene kin.
source: Middle and late Pleistocene forms tended to be smaller in stature than their early Pleistocene kin
evidence: This is a morphological observation from the fossil record.

claim: Middle and late Pleistocene NWSL equids ranged across southern and extreme northwestern North America (i.e. eastern Beringia, which includes Alaska, USA and Yukon Territory, Canada).
source: and ranged across southern and extreme northwestern North America (i.e. eastern Beringia, which includes Alaska, USA and Yukon Territory, Canada).
evidence: This is a geographic distribution statement based on fossil occurrences.

claim: NWSL equids have been assigned to several named species, such as E. conversidens Owen 1869, E. tau Owen 1869, E. francisci Hay (1915), E. calobatus Troxell 1915, and E. (Asinus) cf. kiang.
source: NWSL equids have been assigned to several named species, such as E. conversidens Owen 1869, E. tau Owen 1869, E. francisci Hay (1915), E. calobatus Troxell 1915, and E. (Asinus) cf. kiang
evidence: This is a statement about taxonomic history.

claim: There is considerable confusion and disagreement regarding the taxonomy of NWSL equids.
source: but there is considerable confusion and disagreement regarding their taxonomy.
evidence: This is a characterization of the state of the field.

claim: Some researchers have chosen to refer to NWSL equids collectively as Equus (Hemionus) spp.
source: Consequently, some researchers have chosen to refer to them collectively as Equus (Hemionus) spp. (Guthrie, 2003; Scott, 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some researchers avoid a formal taxonomic designation for NWSL equids altogether.
source: or avoid a formal taxonomic designation altogether (Der Sarkissian et al., 2015; Vilstrup et al., 2013; Weinstock et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Radiocarbon dates from Gypsum Cave, Nevada, confirm that NWSL equids persisted in areas south of the continental ice sheets during the last glacial maximum (~26–19 thousand years before present).
source: Radiocarbon (14C) dates from Gypsum Cave, Nevada, confirm that NWSL equids persisted in areas south of the continental ice sheets during the last glacial maximum (LGM; ~26–19 thousand years before present (ka BP); Clark et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by radiocarbon dating data and a citation.

claim: NWSL equids persisted until near the terminal Pleistocene, ~13 thousand radiocarbon years before present (14C ka BP).
source: until near the terminal Pleistocene, ~13 thousand radiocarbon years before present (14C ka BP) (Weinstock et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by radiocarbon dating data and a citation.

claim: NWSL equids became extinct soon after ~13 14C ka BP, along with their caballine counterparts and most other coeval species of megafauna.
source: soon after which they became extinct, along with their caballine counterparts and most other coeval species of megafauna (Koch and Barnosky, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on megafaunal extinctions.

claim: In unglaciated eastern Beringia, NWSL equids were seemingly extirpated locally during a relatively mild interstadial interval centered on ~31 14C ka BP.
source: This contrasts with dates from unglaciated eastern Beringia, where NWSL equids were seemingly extirpated locally during a relatively mild interstadial interval centered on ~31 14C ka BP (Guthrie, 2003)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Guthrie, 2003.

claim: In eastern Beringia, NWSL equids were extirpated prior to the LGM, final loss of caballine horses, and arrival of humans in the region.
source: thus prior to the LGM (Clark et al., 2009), final loss of caballine horses (Guthrie, 2003; 2006), and arrival of humans in the region (Guthrie, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The apparently discrepant extirpation chronology between NWSL equids south and north of the continental ice sheets implies that their populations responded variably to demographic pressures in different parts of their range.
source: The apparently discrepant extirpation chronology between NWSL equids south and north of the continental ice sheets implies that their populations responded variably to demographic pressures in different parts of their range, which is consistent with results from some other megafauna (Guthrie, 2006; Zazula et al., 2014; Zazula et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to studies on megafaunal population dynamics.

claim: 26 full mitochondrial genomes and 17 partial nuclear genomes from late Pleistocene NWSL equids were analyzed.
source: We analyzed 26 full mitochondrial genomes and 17 partial nuclear genomes from late Pleistocene NWSL equids
evidence: This describes the data analyzed in the study.

claim: Individuals from both eastern Beringia and southern North America form a single well-supported clade that falls outside the diversity of Equus.
source: which revealed that individuals from both eastern Beringia and southern North America form a single well-supported clade that falls outside the diversity of Equus
evidence: This is a primary finding from the phylogenetic analyses.

claim: NWSL equids diverged from the lineage leading to Equus during the latest Miocene or early Pliocene.
source: and diverged from the lineage leading to Equus during the latest Miocene or early Pliocene.
evidence: This is a divergence time estimate from the study's analyses.

claim: The novel and robust phylogenetic placement of NWSL equids warrants the recognition of NWSL equids as a distinct genus, Haringtonhippus.
source: This novel and robust phylogenetic placement warrants the recognition of NWSL equids as a distinct genus, which we here name Haringtonhippus.
evidence: This is a taxonomic conclusion based on the phylogenetic findings.

claim: Based on the earliest-described specimen bearing diagnosable features, francisci Hay is the most well-supported species name.
source: After reviewing potential species names and conducting morphometric and anatomical comparisons, we determined that, based on the earliest-described specimen bearing diagnosable features, francisci Hay is the most well-supported species name.
evidence: This is a taxonomic conclusion based on morphometric and anatomical analyses.

claim: The analyzed NWSL equid specimens are referred to H. francisci.
source: We therefore refer the analyzed NWSL equid specimens to H. francisci.
evidence: This is a taxonomic assignment based on the study's findings.

claim: New radiocarbon dates revealed that H. francisci was extirpated in eastern Beringia ~14 14C ka BP.
source: New radiocarbon dates revealed that H. francisci was extirpated in eastern Beringia ~14 14C ka BP.
evidence: This is based on new radiocarbon dating data from the study.

claim: Whole mitochondrial genomes were reconstructed from 26 NWSL equids and four New World caballine Equus (two E. lambei, two E. cf. scotti).
source: We reconstructed whole mitochondrial genomes from 26 NWSL equids and four New World caballine Equus (two E. lambei, two E. cf. scotti).
evidence: This describes the data generated in the study.

claim: The resulting phylogeny is mostly consistent with previous studies.
source: The resulting phylogeny is mostly consistent with previous studies (Der Sarkissian et al., 2015; Vilstrup et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a comparison to previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: The phylogeny confirms NWSL equid monophyly.
source: including confirmation of NWSL equid monophyly (Weinstock et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a phylogenetic finding supported by a citation.

claim: The study recovers a strongly supported placement of the NWSL equid clade outside of crown group diversity (Equus), but closer to Equus than to Hippidion.
source: However, we recover a strongly supported placement of the NWSL equid clade outside of crown group diversity (Equus), but closer to Equus than to Hippidion (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, Figure 1—source data 1, and Appendix 2—tables 1–2).
evidence: This is a primary phylogenetic finding from the study, supported by figures and data.

claim: Previous palaeogenetic studies placed the NWSL equids within crown group Equus, closer to caballine horses than to non-caballine asses and zebras.
source: In contrast, previous palaeogenetic studies placed the NWSL equids within crown group Equus, closer to caballine horses than to non-caballine asses and zebras (Barrón-Ortiz et al., 2017; Der Sarkissian et al., 2015; Orlando et al., 2008, 2009; Vilstrup et al., 2013; Weinstock et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a description of previous findings, supported by citations.

claim: Previous results were likely due to a combination of outgroup choice and the use of short, incomplete, or problematic mtDNA sequences.
source: These analyses suggested that previous results were likely due to a combination of outgroup choice and the use of short, incomplete, or problematic mtDNA sequences (Appendix 2 and Appendix 2—table 3).
evidence: This is an inference from the study's analyses.

claim: Partial nuclear genomes from 17 NWSL equids were sequenced and compared to a caballine (horse) and a non-caballine (donkey) reference genome.
source: To confirm the mtDNA result that NWSL equids fall outside of crown group equid diversity, we sequenced and compared partial nuclear genomes from 17 NWSL equids to a caballine (horse) and a non-caballine (donkey) reference genome.
evidence: This describes the nuclear genomic data generated and analyzed in the study.

claim: The relative private transversion frequency for NWSL equids was ~1.4–1.5 times greater than that for horse or donkey.
source: We found that the relative private transversion frequency for NWSL equids was ~1.4–1.5 times greater than that for horse or donkey (Appendix 2, Figure 1—source data 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the nuclear genomic analyses, supported by figures and data.

claim: The relative private transversion frequency result supports the placement of NWSL equids as sister to the horse-donkey clade.
source: This result supports the placement of NWSL equids as sister to the horse-donkey clade (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is an inference from the nuclear genomic data, supported by a figure.

claim: The horse-donkey clade is representative of living Equus diversity.
source: the latter of which is representative of living Equus diversity (e.g. [Der Sarkissian et al., 2015; Jónsson et al., 2014])
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The nuclear genomic result is congruent with the mitochondrial genomic analyses.
source: and is therefore congruent with the mitochondrial genomic analyses.
evidence: This is a comparison between the nuclear and mitochondrial results.

claim: The Hippidion-NWSL/Equus split (node 1) is estimated at 5.15–7.66 Ma.
source: This gave divergence estimates for the Hippidion-NWSL/Equus split (node 1) at 5.15–7.66 Ma, consistent with (Der Sarkissian et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a divergence time estimate from the Bayesian time-tree analysis, consistent with a previous study.

claim: The NWSL-Equus split (node 2) is estimated at 4.09–5.13 Ma.
source: the NWSL-Equus split (node 2) at 4.09–5.13 Ma
evidence: This is a divergence time estimate from the Bayesian time-tree analysis.

claim: The caballine/non-caballine Equus split (node 3) is estimated at 3.77–4.40 Ma.
source: and the caballine/non-caballine Equus split (node 3) at 3.77–4.40 Ma (Figure 1 and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a divergence time estimate from the Bayesian time-tree analysis, shown in Figure 1.

claim: The NWSL-Equus mitochondrial split occurred only ~500 thousand years (ka) prior to the caballine/non-caballine Equus split.
source: These estimates suggest that the NWSL-Equus mitochondrial split occurred only ~500 thousand years (ka) prior to the caballine/non-caballine Equus split.
evidence: This is an inference from the divergence time estimates.

claim: The NWSL-Equus divergence time estimated from nuclear genomes is 4.87–5.69 Ma.
source: This analysis yielded a divergence estimate of 4.87–5.69 Ma (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is a divergence time estimate from the nuclear genomic analysis, shown in a figure.

claim: The nuclear genomic divergence estimate overlaps with that obtained from the relaxed clock analysis of whole mitochondrial genome data.
source: which overlaps with that obtained from the relaxed clock analysis of whole mitochondrial genome data (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a comparison between the nuclear and mitochondrial divergence estimates, shown in Figure 1.

claim: The NWSL equid and Equus clades diverged during the latest Miocene or early Pliocene (4.1–5.7 Ma; late Hemphillian or earliest Blancan).
source: These analyses suggest that the NWSL equid and Equus clades diverged during the latest Miocene or early Pliocene (4.1–5.7 Ma; late Hemphillian or earliest Blancan).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the divergence time analyses.

claim: The genus Equus (Linnaeus, 1758) was named to include three living equid groups – horses (E. caballus), donkeys (E. asinus), and zebras (E. zebra) – whose diversity comprises all extant, or crown group, equids.
source: The genus Equus (Linnaeus, 1758) was named to include three living equid groups – horses (E. caballus), donkeys (E. asinus), and zebras (E. zebra) – whose diversity comprises all extant, or crown group, equids.
evidence: This is a statement about the definition of the genus Equus.

claim: Previous palaeontological and palaeogenetic studies have uniformly placed NWSL equids within the diversity of extant equids and therefore the genus Equus.
source: Previous palaeontological and palaeogenetic studies have uniformly placed NWSL equids within the diversity of extant equids and therefore this genus (Barrón-Ortiz et al., 2017; Bennett, 1980; Der Sarkissian et al., 2015; Harington and Clulow, 1973; Orlando et al., 2008; 2009; Scott, 2004; Vilstrup et al., 2013; Weinstock et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The placement of NWSL equids within Equus conflicts with the phylogenetic signal provided by palaeogenomic data.
source: This, however, conflicts with the phylogenetic signal provided by palaeogenomic data, which strongly suggest that NWSL equids fall outside the confines of the equid crown group (Equus).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's palaeogenomic analyses.

claim: There is no morphological or genetic evidence warranting the assignment of NWSL equids to an existing extinct taxon such as Hippidion.
source: Nor is there any morphological or genetic evidence warranting the assignment of NWSL equids to an existing extinct taxon such as Hippidion.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's analyses.

claim: A new genus for NWSL equids, Haringtonhippus, is erected.
source: We therefore erect a new genus for NWSL equids, Haringtonhippus, as defined and delimited below:
evidence: This is a taxonomic action based on the study's findings.

claim: The type species of Haringtonhippus is Haringtonhippus francisci Hay 1915.
source: Type species. Haringtonhippus francisci Hay 1915.
evidence: This is a taxonomic designation.

claim: The new genus Haringtonhippus is named in honor of C. Richard Harington, who first described NWSL equids from eastern Beringia.
source: The new genus is named in honor of C. Richard Harington, who first described NWSL equids from eastern Beringia (Harington and Clulow, 1973).
evidence: This explains the etymology of the genus name, supported by a citation.

claim: The holotype of Haringtonhippus francisci is a partial skeleton consisting of a complete cranium, mandible, and a stilt-legged third metatarsal (MTIII) (TMM 34–2518).
source: A partial skeleton consisting of a complete cranium, mandible, and a stilt-legged third metatarsal (MTIII) (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), which is curated at the Texas Vertebrate Paleontology Collections at The University of Texas, Austin (TMM 34–2518).
evidence: This describes the holotype specimen, with reference to figures.

claim: The holotype specimen (TMM 34–2518) is from the middle Pleistocene Lissie Formation of Wharton County, Texas.
source: This specimen is the holotype of 'E'. francisci, originally described by Hay (1915), and is from the middle Pleistocene Lissie Formation of Wharton County, Texas (Hay, 1915; Lundelius and Stevens, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original description and subsequent studies.

claim: On the basis of mitochondrial and nuclear genomic data, a cranium, femur, and MTIII (LACM(CIT): Nevada) are assigned to Haringtonhippus.
source: On the basis of mitochondrial and nuclear genomic data, we assign the following material confidently to Haringtonhippus: a cranium, femur, and MTIII (LACM(CIT): Nevada)
evidence: This is a taxonomic assignment based on genomic data.

claim: Three MTIIIs, three third metacarpals (MCIII), three premolar teeth, and a molar tooth (KU: Wyoming) are assigned to Haringtonhippus on the basis of mitochondrial and nuclear genomic data.
source: three MTIIIs, three third metacarpals (MCIII), three premolar teeth, and a molar tooth (KU: Wyoming)
evidence: This is a taxonomic assignment based on genomic data.

claim: Two radii, 12 MTIIIs, three MCIIIs, a metapodial, and a first phalanx (YG: Yukon Territory) are assigned to Haringtonhippus on the basis of mitochondrial and nuclear genomic data.
source: two radii, 12 MTIIIs, three MCIIIs, a metapodial, and a first phalanx (YG: Yukon Territory)
evidence: This is a taxonomic assignment based on genomic data.

claim: A premolar tooth (UTEP: New Mexico) is assigned to Haringtonhippus on the basis of mitochondrial and nuclear genomic data.
source: and a premolar tooth (University of Texas El Paso, UTEP: New Mexico)
evidence: This is a taxonomic assignment based on genomic data.

claim: The referred material includes at least four males and at least six females.
source: This material includes at least four males and at least six females (Appendix 2, Appendix 2—Table 4 and Appendix 2—Table 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on sex determination from the genomic data.

claim: MTIII specimens from Yukon Territory (n = 13), Wyoming (n = 57), and Nevada (n = 4) are assigned to Haringtonhippus on the basis of morphometric analysis.
source: We further assign MTIII specimens from Yukon Territory (n = 13), Wyoming (n = 57), and Nevada (n = 4) to Haringtonhippus on the basis of morphometric analysis (Figure 2c and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a taxonomic assignment based on morphometric analysis, shown in Figure 2c.

claim: A premolar tooth (LACM(CIT): Nuevo Leon), a premolar and a molar (UTEP: New Mexico), and a premolar (RAM/PMA: Alberta) are tentatively assigned to Haringtonhippus on the basis of short mitochondrial DNA sequences.
source: On the basis of short mitochondrial DNA sequences, we tentatively assign to Haringtonhippus a premolar tooth (LACM(CIT): Nuevo Leon); a premolar and a molar (UTEP: New Mexico); and a premolar (Royal Alberta Museum, RAM/PMA: Alberta) (Barrón-Ortiz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a tentative taxonomic assignment based on short mtDNA sequences, supported by a citation.

claim: 19 NWSL equid metapodial specimens from the Fairbanks area, Alaska are tentatively assigned to Haringtonhippus.
source: We also tentatively assign 19 NWSL equid metapodial specimens from the Fairbanks area, Alaska (Guthrie, 2003) to Haringtonhippus, but note that morphometric and/or palaeogenomic analysis would be required to confirm this designation.
evidence: This is a tentative taxonomic assignment, with a note that confirmation is needed, supported by a citation.

claim: Haringtonhippus is known only from the Pleistocene of North America.
source: Haringtonhippus is known only from the Pleistocene of North America (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a statement about the geographic and temporal distribution, shown in Figure 3.

claim: Haringtonhippus is confidently known from the late Pleistocene of Yukon Territory (Klondike region), Wyoming (Natural Trap Cave), Nevada (Gypsum Cave, Mineral Hill Cave), and New Mexico (Dry Cave).
source: In addition to the middle Pleistocene holotype from Texas, Haringtonhippus is confidently known from the late Pleistocene of Yukon Territory (Klondike region), Wyoming (Natural Trap Cave), Nevada (Gypsum Cave, Mineral Hill Cave), and New Mexico (Dry Cave)
evidence: This is a statement about the geographic distribution based on the study's findings.

claim: Haringtonhippus is tentatively registered as present in Nuevo Leon (San Josecito Cave), Alberta (Edmonton area), and Alaska (Fairbanks area).
source: and is tentatively registered as present in Nuevo Leon (San Josecito Cave), Alberta (Edmonton area), and Alaska (Fairbanks area) (Appendix 2, Supplementary file 1, and Appendix 2—table 3; [Barrón-Ortiz et al., 2017; Vilstrup et al., 2013; Weinstock et al., 2005]).
evidence: This is a tentative statement about the geographic distribution, supported by citations.

claim: New radiocarbon dates were obtained from 17 Yukon Territory fossils.
source: To investigate the last appearance date (LAD) of Haringtonhippus in eastern Beringia, we obtained new radiocarbon dates from 17 Yukon Territory fossils (Appendix 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the radiocarbon dating conducted in the study.

claim: Three statistically-indistinguishable radiocarbon dates of ~14.4 14C ka BP (derived from two independent laboratories) from a metacarpal bone (YG 401.235) of Haringtonhippus represent this taxon's LAD in eastern Beringia.
source: This resulted in three statistically-indistinguishable radiocarbon dates of ~14.4 14C ka BP (derived from two independent laboratories) from a metacarpal bone (YG 401.235) of Haringtonhippus, which represents this taxon's LAD in eastern Beringia (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on new radiocarbon dating data from the study.

claim: The LAD for Haringtonhippus in North America as a whole is based on two dates of ~13.1 14C ka BP from Gypsum Cave, Nevada.
source: The LAD for North America as a whole is based on two dates of ~13.1 14C ka BP from Gypsum Cave, Nevada (Supplementary file 1; [Weinstock et al., 2005]).
evidence: This is based on radiocarbon dates, supported by a citation.

claim: Haringtonhippus is the sister genus to Equus (equid crown group), with Hippidion being sister to the Haringtonhippus-Equus clade.
source: Haringtonhippus is the sister genus to Equus (equid crown group), with Hippidion being sister to the Haringtonhippus-Equus clade (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a phylogenetic finding from the study, shown in Figure 1.

claim: Haringtonhippus can be differentiated from Equus and Hippidion by 178 synapomorphic positions in the mitochondrial genome, including four insertions and 174 substitutions.
source: Haringtonhippus can be differentiated from Equus and Hippidion by 178 synapomorphic positions in the mitochondrial genome, including four insertions and 174 substitutions (Appendix 1—Table 2 and Appendix 1—table 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of mitochondrial genome sequences.

claim: These synapomorphies are tentative and will likely be reduced in number as a greater diversity of mitochondrial genomes for extinct equids become available.
source: We caution that these synapomorphies are tentative and will likely be reduced in number as a greater diversity of mitochondrial genomes for extinct equids become available.
evidence: This is a cautionary note about the interpretation of the synapomorphies.

claim: Using logistic regression on principal components, a strong separation between caballine/stout-legged Equus and stilt-legged equids (hemionine/stilt-legged Equus, Haringtonhippus) MTIIIs can be correctly distinguished with 98.2% accuracy.
source: Using logistic regression on principal components, we find a strong separation that can be correctly distinguished with 98.2% accuracy (Appendix 2; Heintzman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from the morphometric analysis.

claim: Hemionine/stilt-legged Equus MTIIIs occupy the same morphospace as H. francisci in the analysis.
source: Hemionine/stilt-legged Equus MTIIIs occupy the same morphospace as H. francisci in our analysis
evidence: This is a finding from the morphometric analysis.

claim: Given a larger sample size, it may be possible to discriminate E. hemionus from the remaining stilt-legged equids.
source: although given a larger sample size, it may be possible to discriminate E. hemionus from the remaining stilt-legged equids.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future analyses.

claim: Haringtonhippus seems to exhibit a negative correlation between latitude and MTIII length.
source: We note that Haringtonhippus seems to exhibit a negative correlation between latitude and MTIII length
evidence: This is an observation from the morphometric analysis.

claim: Specimens from the same latitude occupy similar morphospace regardless of whether DNA- or morphological-based identification was used.
source: and that specimens from the same latitude occupy similar morphospace regardless of whether DNA- or morphological-based identification was used (Figure 2c and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the morphometric analysis, shown in Figure 2c.

claim: On the basis of morphology, all confidently referred material of Haringtonhippus is assigned to the single species H. francisci Hay (1915).
source: On the basis of morphology, we assign all confidently referred material of Haringtonhippus to the single species H. francisci Hay (1915) (Appendix 2).
evidence: This is a taxonomic conclusion based on morphological analysis.

claim: Comparison between the cranial anatomical features of LACM(CIT) 109/156450 and TMM 34–2518 reveal some minor differences, which can likely be ascribed to intraspecific variation.
source: Comparison between the cranial anatomical features of LACM(CIT) 109/156450 and TMM 34–2518 reveal some minor differences, which can likely be ascribed to intraspecific variation (Figure 2a and Appendix 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference from morphological comparison, shown in figures.

claim: The MTIII of TMM 34–2518 is comparable to the MTIIIs ascribed to Haringtonhippus by palaeogenomic data.
source: Further, the MTIII of TMM 34–2518 is comparable to the MTIIIs ascribed to Haringtonhippus by palaeogenomic data
evidence: This is a morphological comparison.

claim: The MTIII of TMM 34–2518 is consistent with the observed latitudinally correlated variation in MTIII length across Haringtonhippus.
source: and is consistent with the observed latitudinally correlated variation in MTIII length across Haringtonhippus (Figure 2c and Appendix 2).
evidence: This is a morphological comparison, shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The mitochondrial tree topology within Haringtonhippus does not exhibit phylogeographic structure.
source: The mitochondrial tree topology within Haringtonhippus does not exhibit phylogeographic structure (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: This is a finding from the phylogenetic analysis, shown in a figure.

claim: The lack of mitochondrial phylogeographic structure is consistent with sampled Haringtonhippus mitochondrial genomes belonging to the same species.
source: which is consistent with sampled Haringtonhippus mitochondrial genomes belonging to the same species.
evidence: This is an inference from the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The tMRCA for the sampled Haringtonhippus mitochondrial genomes is estimated at ~200–470 ka BP.
source: Using Bayesian time-tree analysis, we estimated a tMRCA for the sampled Haringtonhippus mitochondrial genomes of ~200–470 ka BP (Figure 1 and Figure 1—source data 1; Heintzman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a divergence time estimate from the Bayesian time-tree analysis, shown in Figure 1.

claim: The MRCA of Haringtonhippus is more recent than that of other extant equid species (such as E. asinus and E. quagga, which have a combined 95% HPD range: 410–1030 ka BP).
source: The MRCA of Haringtonhippus is therefore more recent than that of other extant equid species (such as E. asinus and E. quagga, which have a combined 95% HPD range: 410–1030 ka BP; Figure 1 and Figure 1—source data 1; Heintzman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison of divergence time estimates, shown in Figure 1.

claim: The middle Pleistocene holotype TMM 34–2518 (~125–780 ka BP) may predate the Haringtonhippus mitochondrial tMRCA.
source: Although the middle Pleistocene holotype TMM 34–2518 (~125–780 ka BP) may predate our Haringtonhippus mitochondrial tMRCA
evidence: This is a comparison of the holotype age to the tMRCA estimate.

claim: The holotype sample (TMM 34–2518) has no direct date and the range of possible ages falls within the tMRCA range of other extant equid species.
source: this sample has no direct date and the range of possible ages falls within the tMRCA range of other extant equid species.
evidence: This is a statement about the dating of the holotype.

claim: The hypothesis of conspecificity of TMM 34–2518 with Haringtonhippus, as defined palaeogenomically, cannot be rejected.
source: We therefore cannot reject the hypothesis of its conspecificity with Haringtonhippus, as defined palaeogenomically.
evidence: This is an inference from the dating and tMRCA analyses.

claim: Attempts to recover either collagen or genomic data from TMM 34–2518 were unsuccessful.
source: We attempted, but were unable, to recover either collagen or genomic data from TMM 34–2518 (Appendix 2)
evidence: This describes the results of attempts to extract molecular data.

claim: The inability to recover molecular data from TMM 34–2518 is consistent with the taphonomic, stratigraphic, and geographic context of this fossil.
source: consistent with the taphonomic, stratigraphic, and geographic context of this fossil (Hay, 1915; Lundelius and Stevens, 1970).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations.

claim: The molecular evidence is consistent with the assignment of H. francisci as the type and only species of Haringtonhippus.
source: Altogether, the molecular evidence is consistent with the assignment of H. francisci as the type and only species of Haringtonhippus.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the molecular analyses.

claim: The suggested placement of NWSL equids within a taxon (Haringtonhippus) sister to Equus is a departure from previous interpretations.
source: The suggested placement of NWSL equids within a taxon (Haringtonhippus) sister to Equus is a departure from previous interpretations, which variably place the former within Equus, as sister to hemionines or caballine horses (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous interpretations, shown in Figure 1.

claim: The earliest equids exhibiting morphologies consistent with NWSL and caballine attribution appear in the fossil record only ~2–3 and ~1.9–0.7 Ma ago, respectively.
source: According to broadly accepted palaeontological interpretations, the earliest equids exhibiting morphologies consistent with NWSL and caballine attribution appear in the fossil record only ~2–3 and ~1.9–0.7 Ma ago (Eisenmann et al., 2008; Forsten, 1992), respectively
evidence: This is supported by citations to paleontological studies.

claim: Divergence estimates suggest that the NWSL and caballine lineages diverged between 4.1–5.8 and 3.8–4.5 Ma, most likely in North America.
source: whereas our divergence estimates suggest that these lineages to have diverged between 4.1–5.8 and 3.8–4.5 Ma, most likely in North America.
evidence: This is a divergence time estimate from the study's analyses.

claim: Dating incongruence might be attributed to an incomplete fossil record, but this seems unlikely given the density of the record for late Neogene and Pleistocene horses.
source: Dating incongruence might be attributed to an incomplete fossil record, but this seems unlikely given the density of the record for late Neogene and Pleistocene horses.
evidence: This is a discussion of potential explanations for the incongruence.

claim: The NWSL-Equus split is robustly calibrated to the caballine/non-caballine Equus divergence at 4.0–4.5 Ma, which is in turn derived from a direct molecular clock calibration using a middle Pleistocene horse genome.
source: However, we emphasize that the NWSL-Equus split is robustly calibrated to the caballine/non-caballine Equus divergence at 4.0–4.5 Ma, which is in turn derived from a direct molecular clock calibration using a middle Pleistocene horse genome (Orlando et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about the calibration of the divergence time estimates, supported by a citation.

claim: Incongruence between fossil and genomic dating might be attributed to discordance between the timing of species divergence and the evolution of diagnostic anatomical characteristics, or failure to detect or account for homoplasy.
source: Other possibilities to explain the incongruence include discordance between the timing of species divergence and the evolution of diagnostic anatomical characteristics, or failure to detect or account for homoplasy (Forsten, 1992).
evidence: This is a discussion of potential explanations, supported by a citation.

claim: Pliocene Equus generally exhibits a primitive ('plesippine' in North America, 'stenonid' in the Old World) morphology that presages living zebras and asses.
source: For example, Pliocene Equus generally exhibits a primitive ('plesippine' in North America, 'stenonid' in the Old World) morphology that presages living zebras and asses (Forsten, 1988, 1992)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Forsten's work.

claim: More derived caballine (stout-legged) and hemionine (stilt-legged) forms evolved in the early Pleistocene.
source: with more derived caballine (stout-legged) and hemionine (stilt-legged) forms evolving in the early Pleistocene.
evidence: This is a statement about equid evolution.

claim: The stilt-legged morphology appears to have evolved independently at least once in each of the Old and New Worlds, yielding the Asiatic wild asses and Haringtonhippus, respectively.
source: The stilt-legged morphology appears to have evolved independently at least once in each of the Old and New Worlds, yielding the Asiatic wild asses and Haringtonhippus, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference from the phylogenetic and morphological analyses.

claim: The middle-late Pleistocene Eurasian E. hydruntinus is included within the Asiatic wild asses.
source: We include the middle-late Pleistocene Eurasian E. hydruntinus within the Asiatic wild asses (following [Bennett et al., 2017; Burke et al., 2003; Orlando et al., 2006])
evidence: This is a taxonomic assignment supported by citations.

claim: The Old World sussemione E. ovodovi may represent another instance of independent stilt-legged origin, but its relation to Asiatic wild asses and other non-caballine Equus is currently unresolved.
source: and note that the Old World sussemione E. ovodovi may represent another instance of independent stilt-legged origin, but its relation to Asiatic wild asses and other non-caballine Equus is currently unresolved (as depicted in Der Sarkissian et al., 2015; Orlando et al., 2009; Vilstrup et al., 2013; and Figure 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the uncertain phylogenetic position of E. ovodovi, supported by citations and Figure 1.

claim: It is plausible that features at the plesiomorphous end of the spectrum, such as those associated with Hippidion, survived after the early to middle Pleistocene at lower latitudes (South America, Africa).
source: It is plausible that features at the plesiomorphous end of the spectrum, such as those associated with Hippidion, survived after the early to middle Pleistocene at lower latitudes (South America, Africa; Figure 1).
evidence: This is a speculative statement, shown in Figure 1.

claim: The more derived hemionine and caballine morphologies evolved from, and replaced, their antecedents in higher latitude North America and Eurasia, perhaps as adaptations to the extreme ecological pressures perpetuated by the advance and retreat of continental ice sheets and correlated climate oscillations during the Pleistocene.
source: By contrast, the more derived hemionine and caballine morphologies evolved from, and replaced, their antecedents in higher latitude North America and Eurasia, perhaps as adaptations to the extreme ecological pressures perpetuated by the advance and retreat of continental ice sheets and correlated climate oscillations during the Pleistocene (Forsten, 1992, Forsten, 1996Forsten, 1996).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The high-latitude replacement model is consistent with the turnover observed in regional fossil records for Pleistocene equids in North America and Eurasia.
source: We note that this high-latitude replacement model is consistent with the turnover observed in regional fossil records for Pleistocene equids in North America (Azzaroli, 1992; Azzaroli and Voorhies, 1993) and Eurasia (Forsten, 1988, 1992, Forsten, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to paleontological studies.

claim: In South America Hippidion co-existed with caballine horses until they both succumbed to extinction, together with much of the New World megafauna near the end of the Pleistocene.
source: By contrast, in South America Hippidion co-existed with caballine horses until they both succumbed to extinction, together with much of the New World megafauna near the end of the Pleistocene (Forsten, 1996; Koch and Barnosky, 2006; O'Dea et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on South American megafaunal extinctions.

claim: The high-latitude replacement model helps to explain the discordance between the timings of the appearance of the caballine and hemionine morphologies in the fossil record and the divergence of lineages leading to these forms as estimated from palaeogenomic data.
source: This model helps to explain the discordance between the timings of the appearance of the caballine and hemionine morphologies in the fossil record and the divergence of lineages leading to these forms as estimated from palaeogenomic data.
evidence: This is an inference from the proposed model.

claim: The high-latitude replacement model predicts that some previously described North American Pliocene and early Pleistocene Equus species (e.g. E. simplicidens, E. idahoensis), or specimens thereof, may be ancestral to extant Equus and/or late Pleistocene Haringtonhippus.
source: this model predicts that some previously described North American Pliocene and early Pleistocene Equus species (e.g. E. simplicidens, E. idahoensis; [Azzaroli and Voorhies, 1993]), or specimens thereof, may be ancestral to extant Equus and/or late Pleistocene Haringtonhippus.
evidence: This is a prediction from the proposed model, supported by a citation.

claim: Three new radiocarbon dates of ~14.4 14C ka BP from a Yukon Haringtonhippus fossil greatly extends the known temporal range of this genus in eastern Beringia.
source: Three new radiocarbon dates of ~14.4 14C ka BP from a Yukon Haringtonhippus fossil greatly extends the known temporal range of this genus in eastern Beringia.
evidence: This is based on new radiocarbon dating data from the study.

claim: The new radiocarbon dates demonstrate, contrary to the previous LAD of 31,400 ± 1200 14C years ago, that Haringtonhippus survived throughout the last glacial maximum in eastern Beringia.
source: This result demonstrates, contrary to its previous LAD of 31,400 ± 1200 14C years ago (AA 26780; [Guthrie, 2003]), that Haringtonhippus survived throughout the last glacial maximum in eastern Beringia (Clark et al., 2009)
evidence: This is a conclusion from the new radiocarbon dating data, supported by citations.

claim: Haringtonhippus may have come into contact with humans near the end of the Pleistocene.
source: and may have come into contact with humans near the end of the Pleistocene (Goebel et al., 2008; Guthrie, 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citations.

claim: The new data suggest that populations of stilt-legged Haringtonhippus and stout-legged caballine Equus were sympatric, both north and south of the continental ice sheets, through the late Pleistocene and became extinct at roughly the same time.
source: These data suggest that populations of stilt-legged Haringtonhippus and stout-legged caballine Equus were sympatric, both north and south of the continental ice sheets, through the late Pleistocene and became extinct at roughly the same time.
evidence: This is an inference from the radiocarbon dating data.

claim: The near synchronous extinction of both horse groups across their entire range in North America suggests that similar causal mechanisms may have led each to their demise.
source: The near synchronous extinction of both horse groups across their entire range in North America suggests that similar causal mechanisms may have led each to their demise.
evidence: This is a speculative inference from the extinction timing data.

claim: Extant members of the genus Equus vary considerably in the sequence of Prdm9, a gene involved in the speciation process, and chromosome number (karyotype).
source: Extant members of the genus Equus vary considerably in the sequence of Prdm9, a gene involved in the speciation process, and chromosome number (karyotype) (Ryder et al., 1978; Steiner and Ryder, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: Extant caballine and non-caballine Equus rarely produce fertile offspring.
source: and extant caballine and non-caballine Equus rarely produce fertile offspring (Allen and Short, 1997; Steiner and Ryder, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: It is unlikely that the more deeply diverged Haringtonhippus and caballine Equus would have been able to hybridize.
source: It is unlikely, therefore, that the more deeply diverged Haringtonhippus and caballine Equus would have been able to hybridize.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic divergence and reproductive isolation data.

claim: Future analysis of high coverage nuclear genomes, ideally including an outgroup such as Hippidion, will make it possible to test for admixture that may have occurred soon after the lineages leading to Haringtonhippus and Equus diverged.
source: Future analysis of high coverage nuclear genomes, ideally including an outgroup such as Hippidion, will make it possible to test for admixture that may have occurred soon after the lineages leading to Haringtonhippus and Equus diverged, as occurred between the early caballine and non-caballine Equus lineages (Jónsson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about future research possibilities, supported by a citation.

claim: It may be possible to use isotopic and/or tooth mesowear analyses to assess the potential of resource partitioning between Haringtonhippus and caballine Equus in the New World.
source: It may also be possible to use isotopic and/or tooth mesowear analyses to assess the potential of resource partitioning between Haringtonhippus and caballine Equus in the New World.
evidence: This is a statement about future research possibilities.

claim: Fossils of NWSL equids have been known for more than a century, but until the present study their systematic position within Plio-Pleistocene Equidae was poorly characterized.
source: Fossils of NWSL equids have been known for more than a century, but until the present study their systematic position within Plio-Pleistocene Equidae was poorly characterized.
evidence: This is a statement about the history of NWSL equid research.

claim: Detailed anatomical studies strongly indicated that what we now call Haringtonhippus was related to Asiatic wild asses, such as Tibetan khulan and Persian onagers, rather than to caballine horses.
source: This was not because of a lack of interest on the part of earlier workers, whose detailed anatomical studies strongly indicated that what we now call Haringtonhippus was related to Asiatic wild asses, such as Tibetan khulan and Persian onagers, rather than to caballine horses (Eisenmann et al., 2008; Guthrie, 2003; Scott, 2004; Skinner and Hibbard, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The cues of morphology have turned out to be misleading in the case of NWSL equids.
source: That the cues of morphology have turned out to be misleading in this case underlines a recurrent problem in systematic biology
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: There is a recurrent problem in systematic biology of how best to discriminate authentic relationships within groups, such as Neogene equids, that were prone to rampant convergence.
source: which is how best to discriminate authentic relationships within groups, such as Neogene equids, that were prone to rampant convergence.
evidence: This is a general statement about systematic biology.

claim: The solution adopted in this study was to utilize both palaeogenomic and morphometric information in reframing the position of Haringtonhippus.
source: The solution we adopted here was to utilize both palaeogenomic and morphometric information in reframing the position of Haringtonhippus
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: Haringtonhippus now clearly emerges as the closest known outgroup to all living Equus.
source: which now clearly emerges as the closest known outgroup to all living Equus.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's phylogenetic analyses.

claim: An approach which incorporates phenomics with molecular methods (palaeogenomic as well as palaeoproteomic) is likely to offer a means for securely detecting relationships within speciose groups that are highly diverse ecomorphologically.
source: Our success in this regard demonstrates that an approach which incorporates phenomics with molecular methods (palaeogenomic as well as palaeoproteomic, e.g. [Welker et al., 2015]) is likely to offer a means for securely detecting relationships within speciose groups that are highly diverse ecomorphologically.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about methodological approaches, supported by a citation.

claim: Taphonomic degradation is the critical limit for molecular approaches.
source: All methods have their limits, with taphonomic degradation being the critical one for molecular approaches.
evidence: This is a general statement about the limitations of molecular methods.

claim: Proteins may persist significantly longer than ancient DNA.
source: However, proteins may persist significantly longer than ancient DNA (e.g. [Rybczynski et al., 2013])
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Collagen proteomics may come to play a key role in characterizing affinities, as well as the reality, of several proposed Neogene equine taxa (e.g. Dinohippus, Pliohippus, Protohippus, Calippus, and Astrohippus) whose distinctiveness and relationships are far from settled.
source: and collagen proteomics may come to play a key role in characterizing affinities, as well as the reality, of several proposed Neogene equine taxa (e.g. Dinohippus, Pliohippus, Protohippus, Calippus, and Astrohippus; [MacFadden, 1998]) whose distinctiveness and relationships are far from settled (Azzaroli and Voorhies, 1993; Forsten, 1992).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research, supported by citations.

claim: A reciprocally informative approach like the one taken in this study holds much promise for lessening the amount of systematic noise, due to oversplitting, that hampers our understanding of the evolutionary biology of other major late Pleistocene megafaunal groups such as bison and mammoths.
source: A reciprocally informative approach like the one taken here holds much promise for lessening the amount of systematic noise, due to oversplitting, that hampers our understanding of the evolutionary biology of other major late Pleistocene megafaunal groups such as bison and mammoths (Enk et al., 2016; Froese et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a general conclusion about the broader implications of the study's approach, supported by citations.

claim: The combined genomic and phenomic approach is clearly capable of providing new insights into just how extensive megafaunal losses were at the end of the Pleistocene, in what might be justifiably called the opening act of the Sixth Mass Extinction in North America.
source: This approach is clearly capable of providing new insights into just how extensive megafaunal losses were at the end of the Pleistocene, in what might be justifiably called the opening act of the Sixth Mass Extinction in North America.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about the broader implications of the study.

claim: Yukon fossil material (17 Haringtonhippus francisci, two Equus cf. scotti, and two E. lambei) was recovered from active placer mines in the Klondike goldfields near Dawson City.
source: We recovered Yukon fossil material (17 Haringtonhippus francisci, two Equus cf. scotti, and two E. lambei; Supplementary file 1) from active placer mines in the Klondike goldfields near Dawson City.
evidence: This describes the sample collection.

claim: Seven H. francisci fossils from the contiguous USA were sampled from collections at the University of Kansas Biodiversity Institute (KU; n = 4), Los Angeles County Museum of Natural History (LACM(CIT); n = 2), and the Texas Vertebrate Paleontology Collections at The University of Texas (TMM; n = 1).
source: We further sampled seven H. francisci fossils from the contiguous USA that are housed in collections at the University of Kansas Biodiversity Institute (KU; n = 4), Los Angeles County Museum of Natural History (LACM(CIT); n = 2), and the Texas Vertebrate Paleontology Collections at The University of Texas (TMM; n = 1).
evidence: This describes the sample collection.

claim: The Klondike fossils and the H. francisci cranium from the LACM(CIT) were radiocarbon dated.
source: We radiocarbon dated the Klondike fossils and the H. francisci cranium from the LACM(CIT) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the radiocarbon dating conducted in the study.

claim: Mitogenomic coverage ranged from 5.8× to 110.7×.
source: resulting in mitogenomic coverage ranging from 5.8× to 110.7× (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the sequencing coverage achieved.

claim: Equid mtDNA could not be recovered from TMM 34–2518 (the francisci holotype) using the enrichment approach.
source: We were unable to recover equid mtDNA from TMM 34–2518 (the francisci holotype) using this approach (Appendix 2).
evidence: This describes the results of attempts to recover mtDNA.

claim: The mtDNA genome sequences were supplemented with 38 previously published complete equid mtDNA genomes.
source: We supplemented our mtDNA genome sequences with 38 previously published complete equid mtDNA genomes.
evidence: This describes the data used in the analyses.

claim: Six alignment data sets were constructed and models of molecular evolution were selected for the analyses.
source: We constructed six alignment data sets and selected models of molecular evolution for the analyses described below (Appendix 1—table 1, and Supplementary file 1; Heintzman et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the data preparation for the analyses.

claim: The phylogenetic position of the NWSL equids (=H. francisci) was tested using mtDNA data sets 1–3 and applying Bayesian and maximum likelihood (ML) analyses.
source: We tested the phylogenetic position of the NWSL equids (=H. francisci) using mtDNA data sets 1–3 and applying Bayesian (Ronquist et al., 2012) and maximum likelihood (ML; [Stamatakis, 2014]) analyses.
evidence: This describes the phylogenetic analyses conducted, supported by citations to the software used.

claim: The outgroup, the inclusion or exclusion of the fast-evolving partitions, and the inclusion or exclusion of Hippidion sequences were varied in the phylogenetic analyses.
source: We varied the outgroup, the inclusion or exclusion of the fast-evolving partitions, and the inclusion or exclusion of Hippidion sequences.
evidence: This describes the variations in the phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Due to the lack of a globally supported topology across the Bayesian and ML phylogenetic analyses, an Evolutionary Placement Algorithm (EPA) was used to determine the a posteriori likelihood of phylogenetic placements for candidate equid outgroups using mtDNA data set four.
source: Due to the lack of a globally supported topology across the Bayesian and ML phylogenetic analyses, we used an Evolutionary Placement Algorithm (EPA; [Berger et al., 2011]) to determine the a posteriori likelihood of phylogenetic placements for candidate equid outgroups using mtDNA data set four.
evidence: This describes the use of EPA to resolve phylogenetic uncertainty, supported by a citation.

claim: The same EPA approach was used to assess the placement of previously published equid sequences.
source: We also used the same approach to assess the placement of previously published equid sequences (Appendix 2).
evidence: This describes the use of EPA to assess previous sequences.

claim: Bayesian timetree analyses were run using mtDNA data set five to infer divergence times between the four major equid groups (Hippidion, NWSL equids, caballine Equus, and non-caballine Equus).
source: To infer divergence times between the four major equid groups (Hippidion, NWSL equids, caballine Equus, and non-caballine Equus), we ran Bayesian timetree analyses (Drummond et al., 2012) using mtDNA data set five.
evidence: This describes the divergence time analyses, supported by a citation to the software used.

claim: The Bayesian timetree analyses were varied by including or excluding fast-evolving partitions, constraining the root height or not, and including or excluding the E. ovodovi sequence.
source: We varied these analyses by including or excluding fast-evolving partitions, constrained the root height or not, and including or excluding the E. ovodovi sequence.
evidence: This describes the variations in the divergence time analyses.

claim: A list of putative synapomorphic base states, including indels and substitutions, that define the genera Hippidion, Haringtonhippus, and Equus at sites across the mtDNA genome was constructed using data set six.
source: To facilitate future identification of equid mtDNA sequences, we constructed, using data set six, a list of putative synapomorphic base states, including indels and substitutions, that define the genera Hippidion, Haringtonhippus, and Equus at sites across the mtDNA genome.
evidence: This describes the construction of a list of synapomorphies.

claim: The nuclear genomes of a horse (EquCab2), donkey, and the shotgun sequence data from 17 NWSL equid samples were compared to test whether the mtDNA genome-based phylogenetic hypothesis truly reflects the species tree.
source: To test whether our mtDNA genome-based phylogenetic hypothesis truly reflects the species tree, we compared the nuclear genomes of a horse (EquCab2), donkey (Orlando et al., 2013), and the shotgun sequence data from 17 of our NWSL equid samples (Figure 1—source data 2, Appendix 1, Appendix 1—figure 1, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the nuclear genomic analyses, supported by a citation.

claim: Four successive approaches were applied to control for reference genome and DNA fragment length biases in the nuclear genomic analyses.
source: We applied four successive approaches, which controlled for reference genome and DNA fragment length biases (Appendix 1).
evidence: This describes the methods used to control for biases in the nuclear genomic analyses.

claim: The divergence between the NWSL equids and Equus (horse and donkey) was estimated by fitting the branch length, or relative private transversion frequency, ratio between horse/donkey and NWSL equids into a simple phylogenetic scenario.
source: We estimated the divergence between the NWSL equids and Equus (horse and donkey) by fitting the branch length, or relative private transversion frequency, ratio between horse/donkey and NWSL equids into a simple phylogenetic scenario (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the method for estimating divergence from nuclear genomes, shown in a figure.

claim: The NWSL equid branch length was multiplied by a previous horse-donkey divergence estimate (4.0–4.5 Ma) to give the estimated NWSL equid-Equus divergence date, assuming a strict genome-wide molecular clock.
source: We then multiplied the NWSL equid branch length by a previous horse-donkey divergence estimate (4.0–4.5 Ma; [Orlando et al., 2013]) to give the estimated NWSL equid-Equus divergence date, following (Heintzman et al., 2015) and assuming a strict genome-wide molecular clock (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes the method for estimating divergence, supported by citations and shown in a figure.

claim: The sex of the 17 NWSL equid samples was determined by comparing the relative mapping frequency of the autosomes to the X chromosome.
source: We determined the sex of the 17 NWSL equid samples by comparing the relative mapping frequency of the autosomes to the X chromosome.
evidence: This describes the method for sex determination.

claim: The prevalence of mitochondrial and nuclear DNA damage in a subset of the equid samples was assessed using mapDamage.
source: We assessed the prevalence of mitochondrial and nuclear DNA damage in a subset of the equid samples using mapDamage (Jónsson et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the DNA damage analysis, supported by a citation to the software used.
